review_basis: Full-resolution inspection of original numbered WebP slides 23–28; source diagrams, side-by-side compute choices, arrows, pricing labels and examples narrated in order.
part_title: AWS Lambda Fundamentals, Event Pipelines, Scheduling and Pricing

scenes.title: Why AWS Lambda
scenes.visual_overview: This side-by-side visual explains when an event-triggered Lambda function is better suited than a persistent EC2 server.
visual_walkthrough: Top S3 upload event triggers Lambda and writes output
Lambda no server management, bounded execution, automatic event scaling
EC2 long-running server comparison and customer OS responsibility
Bottom image resize and distinct output S3 location
Exam distinction event task versus persistent process
scenes.visual_example: A new image uploaded to S3 triggers Lambda to resize the image and save the thumbnail to a separate output location.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use Lambda for suitable short event-driven tasks; use EC2 when a continuously running custom environment is needed.
scenes.narration: This visual asks which compute model fits a small job that only needs to run when something happens. Look at the left architecture first. A new object arriving in Amazon S3 generates an event, Lambda runs processing code, and the result is stored, for example back in S3. The three features below explain why Lambda fits this pattern: no server operating system to manage, execution for bounded short tasks, and scaling as events arrive within service quotas. Now compare the large right-hand panel with Amazon EC2. An EC2 instance is a persistent virtual server whose operating system, updates and application scaling you configure. That approach can be useful for long-running workers or specialized software, but requires more server management. Follow the bottom image example step by step: the user uploads a picture into the source bucket, a Lambda function generates a resized thumbnail, and the thumbnail is written to a different S3 location. A different output prefix or bucket avoids the new output triggering the same function repeatedly. The exam panel closes the comparison: event-driven, short-lived work often suits Lambda, whereas a persistent custom server can suit EC2. Standard Lambda functions have a maximum fifteen-minute execution timeout, so not every workload belongs in a function.

scenes.title: Benefits of AWS Lambda
scenes.visual_overview: A four-benefit comparison surrounds an event-source-to-function architecture for serverless processing.
visual_walkthrough: Top cards: event invocation, scaling, request-plus-duration billing, AWS integrations
Middle S3, EventBridge, CloudWatch arrows into Lambda
Three arrows out: scaling, billing and integrations
Bottom S3 image upload, Lambda extracts metadata, DynamoDB stores results
Exam benefits and scaling/charge caveats
scenes.visual_example: An image uploaded to S3 invokes Lambda to extract labels/text/dimensions and store chosen metadata in DynamoDB.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Lambda reduces server operations but still has concurrency limits, IAM permissions and downstream dependencies.
scenes.narration: This slide explains why developers choose Lambda after deciding that their workload is event driven. The four benefit boxes across the top describe on-demand invocation, automatic scaling, charges for requests and processing duration, and connections to other AWS services. Now follow the large central architecture. Amazon S3 can emit object events; EventBridge can route scheduled or custom events; and supported CloudWatch alarms or logs can initiate workflows. These paths converge on the Lambda function, which runs your application code. The three arrows to the right explain the outcomes: capacity can scale with incoming demand subject to quotas and target limits, billing reflects requests and configured compute resources, and the code can read or write permitted AWS resources. This does not mean every function has unlimited concurrency or zero surrounding cost. The worked example at the bottom is specific: a new image appears in S3, Lambda processes it to obtain metadata such as labels, text or dimensions, then saves the metadata in DynamoDB for later search and analysis. The service-to-service calls need appropriate IAM permissions. Taken together, the slide shows an event source, a short compute action, a stored result, and operational benefits, not a constantly running server.

scenes.title: AWS Lambda Language Support
scenes.visual_overview: How a function's code and dependencies reach Lambda using a managed runtime, custom runtime or compatible container.
visual_walkthrough: Left source code, dependencies and configuration
Three deployment options: managed Python/Node.js/Java/.NET, custom runtime, container image
Arrow into AWS Lambda execution
Lower Python package example
Exam cue selects runtime matching dependencies and Lambda API compatibility
scenes.visual_example: Package Python function code and its required libraries, choose the supported Python managed runtime and deploy it to Lambda.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A container image must still satisfy Lambda runtime rules; it is not identical to running any arbitrary container.
scenes.narration: This diagram is about choosing the software environment that will execute a Lambda function. Start with the code on the left. The checklist reminds us that a function needs its source code, dependencies and configuration, not only a language name. Follow the arrow into the three runtime options in the middle. The first blue panel shows AWS-managed runtimes such as supported versions of Python, Node.js, Java and .NET. AWS supplies the runtime environment, while you still package application dependencies. The purple middle option is a custom runtime. It is useful when your preferred language or environment is not available as a managed runtime, provided your implementation supports the Lambda Runtime API. The orange panel packages the function and libraries in a compatible container image, which may help with custom tools or dependency packaging. All three paths feed the Lambda service on the right; these are alternative delivery options rather than steps you must complete in order. The bottom worked example shows Python code and libraries bundled into a deployment package, attached to a Python runtime and executed by Lambda. The exam cue is straightforward: choose the environment that actually supports your code, and remember that Lambda container images still follow Lambda's execution model and constraints.

scenes.title: Event-Driven Image Processing with Lambda
scenes.visual_overview: This five-stage architecture converts an uploaded picture to a thumbnail while avoiding recursive S3 triggers.
visual_walkthrough: Upload into images/ prefix
S3 object-created event restricted to source prefix
Lambda reads and resizes image
Output to thumbnails/ prefix or second bucket
Optional DynamoDB JSON metadata with keys and timestamp
Purple recursion-prevention warning
scenes.visual_example: An images/photo.jpg upload triggers Lambda, saves thumbnails/photo.jpg and may record both keys and timestamp in DynamoDB.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The workflow must separate trigger and output paths and handle possible repeated event delivery safely.
scenes.narration: This visual is a complete example of event-driven image processing, so follow its five numbered boxes from left to right. A user uploads a photo to the source S3 bucket under the images prefix. S3 emits an object-created notification configured to match that source prefix. Lambda receives the event, reads the original image, resizes it and writes a thumbnail to the thumbnails prefix or to a separate output bucket. The fifth dashed box is optional: DynamoDB can store metadata such as the original key, thumbnail key and time of processing. Now look at the prominent purple warning across the middle. If the new thumbnail is saved into a location that triggers the same event rule, Lambda can invoke itself repeatedly. Keeping input and output prefixes distinct and filtering the notification prevents that accidental loop. The lower worked example traces a landscape picture into a smaller thumbnail, and the JSON card shows concrete fields like originalKey images/photo.jpg and thumbnailKey thumbnails/photo.jpg. Real S3 events can be delivered more than once, so the function should be safe to repeat using an object or version identifier. The overall architecture is S3 event, Lambda transformation, protected output and optional metadata, with the event filter as an essential safety control.

scenes.title: Scheduled Processing with EventBridge and Lambda
scenes.visual_overview: A time-based EventBridge schedule invokes a function that cleans data and records its work.
visual_walkthrough: Top schedule arrow to Lambda then target resources and CloudWatch Logs
Bottom nightly 2:00 AM EventBridge → Lambda → S3 → DynamoDB
Right exam notes about periodic jobs, serverless operation and logs
Retry/time-zone and failure-handling design context
scenes.visual_example: An EventBridge schedule invokes Lambda at 2 AM to delete old S3 files and update metadata in DynamoDB, logging execution to CloudWatch.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The timer triggers the action; Lambda does not run continuously while waiting for the next scheduled job.
scenes.narration: This slide shows an event that is triggered by time rather than by a file upload or user request. Start with the calendar icon at the upper left. An EventBridge schedule produces a time-based event, which follows the arrow to Lambda. The Lambda function performs the task and interacts with target resources on the right, while CloudWatch Logs records execution details used for troubleshooting. A schedule is not a continuously running server; Lambda starts when invoked. Trace the lower practical example. At two in the morning, EventBridge invokes the cleanup function. The code finds and deletes eligible older S3 objects, aggregates metadata, and optionally updates DynamoDB records. The arrows show the sequence of work, while the upper branch explains monitoring. EventBridge Scheduler supports recurring, cron or one-time schedules and can be configured with a time zone, retries and failure destinations as appropriate. The function still needs IAM permission to read, delete or update only the selected resources, and it must be safe if the event is delivered again. The exam bullets emphasize periodic maintenance and logging rather than always-on EC2 capacity. Together, EventBridge supplies timing, Lambda supplies short-lived compute, AWS data services hold the results, and CloudWatch supports diagnosis.

scenes.title: AWS Lambda Pricing: Example
scenes.visual_overview: A diagram of Lambda's request and GB-second charges, with other service costs and a simple thousand-invocation scenario.
visual_walkthrough: Requests enter Lambda function with configured memory
Two priced terms: request count plus duration × memory
Ancillary charges for storage, transfer and surrounding services
1,000 short invocations flow to usage invoice
EC2 always-on versus Lambda pay-for-use comparison
scenes.visual_example: One thousand short invocations incur request and compute-duration usage; other charges may apply depending on resources and logs.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Estimate GB-seconds and request volume at current rates; a raw multiplication of unlike units is only a conceptual diagram.
scenes.narration: This slide separates the different parts of a Lambda bill. Read the upper flow from left to right. An application or AWS service sends invocations to Lambda, and the function runs with a configured memory allocation. The central box shows two charge categories: the number of requests and the time spent executing multiplied by allocated memory. More precisely, compute usage is measured in gigabyte-seconds and priced separately from request count; you do not literally add request counts and seconds as though they were the same unit. The next box adds ancillary charges, such as logs, transfer, storage or services that the function calls. The total-cost panel on the right is a qualitative equation listing those categories, not a price quote. Now follow the worked example below. A function runs one thousand times, each for a short period. The bill depends on those thousand requests, the sum of billed execution time at configured memory, applicable free allowances and surrounding charges. Finally, compare the lower-right cards. EC2 often reserves server capacity while running, including idle periods; Lambda usage is event based, which can be economical for intermittent workloads. Actual regional pricing and concurrency choices determine the result, so the right exam decision is to estimate total usage rather than assume all Lambda workloads are automatically cheaper.
